newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street shares seen opening slightly higher. [CORRECTED 22:31 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Wall Street shares seen opening slightly higher. [CORRECTED 22:31 GMT]

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to open slightly higher Tuesday, with the market tiptoeing along ahead of key data due Wednesday and Thursday, dealers said.

"We are in a holding pattern ahead of data, with a slight up tilt," Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnenstock & Co said. "It should be a day with a bit more balance than we have seen in the past week or so."
On Monday the Dow Industrials halted a steep two-session slide after a rebound in the bond market soothed investor fears over rising long-term interest rates.
Slightly firmer bonds also added support to stocks.
On Wednesday July's U.S. retail sales and producer prices figures are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, followed by July's consumer prices at the same time on Thursday.
"Today the market will be positioning itself for tomorrow's retail sales and producer prices data," Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments said.
Analysts also awaited preliminary second quarter U.S. productivity and unit labor costs, forecast at 0.7 percent and 2.7 percent higher respectively. The data is due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
On Monday the Dow Industrials finished up about 31 points or 0.4 percent at 8062 in a late session rally after being off as many as 67 points.
The Nasdaq composite finished off about 12 points at 1587 due to extended profit taking in high technology stocks.
However, the dollar recovered overnight against the mark and yen, which should help inject a firmer tone into stocks, analysts noted.
The long bond also continued to recover, up 11/32 to yield 6.61 percent. The Standard & Poor's 500 futures index rose 1.40 points to 943.95.

The Wall Street Journal's "Heard on the Street" column said Tuesday that some Wall Street investors wondered if Coca-Cola Co's earnings warning Friday will take momentum out of the broader stock market.
Coke's stock has since slumped by about seven percent.

"We have seen companies warn about future earnings and these companies were self-punished. The percentage of these warnings is still rather small," Westfalia's (corrects company from Fahnestock & Co) Cardillo said.
More companies will need to issue profit warnings to signal any new trend in the stock market, Cardillo added.

The dollar was firmer overnight against the yen in Tokyo but dealings were thin. It was trading at 116.20/30. In Europe, the dollar also firmed against the mark, moving back above 1.86 to 1.8620/25 marks.
Japan's Nikkei 225 index closed up 274.93, or 1.46 percent, at 19,099.11.
Tokyo stocks recovered from Monday's plunge of almost four percent, as stability in the dollar and U.S. stocks.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 13.8 at 5045.7.
U.S. stocks in London were mixed with drug company shares hit and Coca-Cola clawing back from its recent drop.

The New York Times, in its marketplace column, said Wall Street was waiting for the Securities and Exchange Commission's report on so-called soft dollars, or money stemming from the original fees investors pay money managers. Many in the securities business expect the SEC to call for much more disclosure to investors about soft-dollar arrangements, the column said.
((Wall Street desk 212-859-1730))
